definition.text: Sir Partha Dasgupta (born 1942) is an Indian-British economist at the University of Cambridge whose long-standing interest is ecological economics.

facts.text: With Karl-Göran Mäler he developed 'inclusive wealth' as a measure of human well-being.
His 1982 monograph The Control of Resources set a research agenda linking population, consumption and the natural environment.
He led The Economics of Biodiversity: The Dasgupta Review, commissioned by the UK government and published in February 2021.
The Review aimed at a measure of natural capital usable in judging investment projects and the sustainability of economic programmes.
The Review rebuilds growth, development and poverty economics on the view that the human economy is embedded in Nature, not external to it.
He helped set up the journal Environment and Development Economics in 1996.

title: Pavan Sukhdev

definition.text: Pavan Sukhdev (born 1960) is an Indian environmental economist working on the green economy, biodiversity, natural capital and sustainable finance.

facts.text: He was Study Leader of TEEB (The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity), a G8+5 study hosted by UNEP.
TEEB's 2008 Interim Report showed the economic significance of losing nature's services and linked it to ethics, equity and poverty reduction.
He headed UNEP's Green Economy Initiative, which argued that greening economies drives wealth, jobs and poverty reduction rather than burdening growth.
A banker by background, he spent 14 years at Deutsche Bank and was president of WWF International from 2017 to 2021.

prerequisites: The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity

definition.text: Robert Costanza (born 1950) is an American/Australian ecological economist at University College London's Institute for Global Prosperity.

facts.text: He co-founded the International Society for Ecological Economics, was its first president, and was founding chief editor of its journal Ecological Economics from 1989 to 2002.
In 1997 he led an attempted valuation of the global ecosystem, published in Nature.
The study put the value of ecosystem services at $33 trillion a year, within a range of $16 trillion to $54 trillion, when global GDP was $27 trillion.
Half of that value came from nutrient cycling.
His work lumped ecosystem goods and services together as ecosystem services, unlike Gretchen Daily's original definition.
He studied under H.T. Odum and directed the Gund Institute for Ecological Economics at the University of Vermont.
